section.title: The Plot against Jeremiah
section.sectionRationale: Jeremiah discovers a murder plot from his own hometown, led like a lamb to slaughter without knowing it, and pours out to God the first of his confessions, why do the wicked prosper? God's own answer turns personal: He too has been forsaken by His beloved inheritance, yet even in decreeing uprooting He promises compassion and restoration to come.
section.thesis: Jeremiah's own townsmen conspire to kill him for faithfully speaking God's word, and his honest complaint to God about the prosperity of the wicked is met not with a simple answer but with God's own greater grief over a people who have forsaken Him, though even here uprooting is not God's last word, since compassion and restoration remain promised.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the murder plot against Jeremiah uncovered and judgment pronounced on the men of Anathoth; Jeremiah's honest complaint that the wicked prosper while he suffers for faithfulness; God's own lament that His beloved inheritance has forsaken Him and become like a lion roaring against Him; and a final word of hope, that even the nations uprooted for cruelty may yet be established among God's people if they turn to Him.

verses.text: And the LORD informed me, so I knew. Then You showed me their deeds.

For I was like a gentle {{kebes|lamb}} led to slaughter; I did not know that they had plotted against me: “Let us destroy the tree with its fruit; let us cut him off from the land of the living, 
that his name may be remembered no more.”
O LORD of Hosts, who judges righteously, who examines the heart and mind, let me see Your vengeance upon them, for to You I have committed my cause.
Therefore this is what the LORD says concerning the people of Anathoth who are seeking your life and saying, “You must not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand.”
So this is what the LORD of Hosts says: “I will punish them. Their young men will die by the sword, their sons and daughters by famine.
There will be no remnant, for I will bring disaster on the people of Anathoth in the year of their punishment.”

units.label: Why does the way of the wicked prosper?

verses.text:
Righteous are You, O LORD, when I plead before You. Yet about Your judgments I wish to {{rib|contend}} with You: 
Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all the faithless live at ease?
You planted them, and they have taken root. They have grown and produced fruit. You are ever on their lips, but far from their hearts.
But You know me, O LORD; You see me and test my heart toward You. Drag away the wicked like sheep to the slaughter and set them apart for the day of carnage.

How long will the land mourn and the grass of every field be withered? Because of the evil of its residents, the animals and birds have been swept away, for the people have said, “He cannot see what our end will be.”

“If you have raced with men on foot and they have worn you out, 
how can you compete with horses? If you stumble in a peaceful land, how will you do in the thickets of the Jordan?
Even your brothers, your own father’s household, even they have betrayed you; even they have cried aloud against you. Do not trust them, though they speak well of you.

units.label: I have forsaken My house
units.note: God's own grief over His inheritance

verses.text: I have forsaken My house; I have abandoned My {{nachalah|inheritance}}; I have given the love of My life into the hands of her enemies.
My inheritance has become to Me like a lion in the forest. She has roared against Me; therefore I hate her.

Is not My inheritance to Me like a speckled bird of prey 
with other birds of prey circling against her? Go, gather all the beasts of the field; bring them to devour her.
Many shepherds have destroyed My vineyard; they have trampled My plot of ground. They have turned My pleasant field into a desolate wasteland.
They have made it a desolation; desolate before Me, it mourns. All the land is laid waste, but no man takes it to heart.

Over all the barren heights in the wilderness the destroyers have come, for the sword of the LORD devours from one end of the earth to the other. 
No flesh has peace.
They have sown wheat but harvested thorns. They have exhausted themselves to no avail. Bear the shame of your harvest because of the fierce anger of the LORD.”

units.label: I will have compassion
units.note: uprooting is not the last word

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “As for all My evil neighbors who attack the inheritance that I bequeathed to My people Israel, I am about to {{nathash|uproot}} them from their land, and I will uproot the house of Judah from among them.
But after I have uprooted them, I will once again have compassion on them and return each one to his inheritance and to his land.

And if they will diligently learn the ways of My people and swear by My name, saying, ‘As surely as the LORD lives’, just as they once taught My people to swear by Baal, then they will be established among My people.
But if they will not obey, then I will uproot that nation; I will uproot it and destroy it, declares the LORD.”

kebes.gloss: A young, gentle lamb. Jeremiah pictures himself led to slaughter without suspecting it, an image later fulfilled supremely in the suffering servant of Isaiah 53:7 and in Christ, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.

rib.gloss: To contend, to bring a legal dispute or lawsuit. Jeremiah uses courtroom language to bring his honest complaint about the prosperity of the wicked directly before God, modeling faith that argues with God rather than abandoning Him in silence.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, a possession given and kept within a family. God repeatedly calls Israel My inheritance in this passage, showing that even in judgment, the relationship of belonging is not simply erased but grieved over as a real loss.

nathash.gloss: To uproot, pluck up, or tear out, a word Jeremiah uses often for both Israel's judgment and the nations'. Strikingly, the same word that decrees uprooting here also frames the promise of compassion and restoration that follows it.

basic.context: Jeremiah learns that the men of his own hometown, Anathoth, have plotted to kill him for prophesying in the LORD's name, and he had not even suspected it, like a gentle lamb led to slaughter. He commits his cause to God and brings the first of his personal confessions recorded in this book, an honest complaint that the wicked prosper while the faithful suffer. God's answer does not simply explain the injustice; it reveals His own grief, since He too has been abandoned by the very people He calls His inheritance.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the first of several raw, personal laments Jeremiah brings directly to God through chapters 11 to 20, showing that honest complaint, even bordering on accusation, has a legitimate place within a life of faith when brought to God rather than nursed in bitterness apart from Him. God's response, in effect you have not seen anything yet, is less an explanation of theodicy than a call to deeper endurance grounded in God's own greater sorrow.
basic.originalLanguages: Jeremiah describes himself as a kebes, gentle lamb, led unknowingly to slaughter, an image later fulfilled in Christ. He tells God he wishes to rib, contend or bring a legal case, over the prosperity of the wicked. God answers by naming Judah His own nachalah, inheritance, now turned against Him, yet still decrees to nathash, uproot, and then, remarkably, promises to have compassion and restore.
basic.typology: Jeremiah as a lamb led to slaughter without knowing it anticipates Isaiah's suffering servant and finds its fullest fulfillment in Christ, the Lamb of God led to the cross. Jeremiah's honest legal complaint against apparent injustice anticipates the pattern of lament fulfilled and absorbed into the cross, where the righteous One suffers unjustly yet entrusts Himself to the Father's justice.
basic.christ: Jeremiah's description of himself as a lamb led to slaughter without knowing it is picked up by Isaiah's suffering servant, He was led like a lamb to the slaughter, Isaiah 53:7, and fulfilled in Jesus, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, John 1:29, who like Jeremiah faced a conspiracy of His own people yet entrusted Himself to the Father who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23.
basic.god: God is not distant from His prophet's suffering; He examines the heart and mind and receives Jeremiah's raw complaint without rebuking his honesty. Yet the deeper revelation here is God's own anguish: He calls Israel the love of My life, given into her enemies' hands, showing that His judgment is never coldly administered but flows from a wounded covenant love. Even His decree to uproot ends with a promise of compassion for those who will turn to Him.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53:7 pictures the servant as a lamb led to slaughter, the image Jeremiah first uses of himself. John 1:29 identifies Jesus as this Lamb. 1 Peter 2:23 describes Christ entrusting Himself to the Father who judges justly, exactly what Jeremiah does in 11:20. Habakkuk 1:2-4 voices the same complaint about the prosperity of the wicked.
basic.oneStory: This is the pattern of the righteous sufferer who cries out honestly to God amid undeserved persecution, a pattern running from Jeremiah through the Psalms of lament to its fullest expression in Christ, the true Lamb led to slaughter, who bore the world's injustice while trusting the Father's just judgment, and who secures the very compassion and restoration promised even to uprooted nations at the end of this passage.

context.literary:
This unit joins two things that the book wants us to read together: the first of Jeremiah's private prayers, which scholars call his confessions, and a poem in which God Himself speaks of grief. The movement is a conversation. Verses 11:18 to 20 are the prophet's cry, 11:21 to 23 is God's verdict on Anathoth, 12:1 to 4 is the complaint, 12:5 to 6 is God's reply, 12:7 to 13 is a lament in God's own voice, and 12:14 to 17 is an oracle that turns toward the nations. Each speaker answers the one before.

Several threads tie the pieces. The first is knowing. 'The LORD informed me, so I knew,' 11:18, and 'You know me, O LORD,' 12:3, are matched by the people's claim in 12:4 that God 'cannot see what our end will be.' The second is slaughter. Jeremiah is a lamb led to slaughter in 11:19, and in 12:3 he asks that the wicked be dragged off 'like sheep to the slaughter.' The same word for slaughter is given to him as a victim and requested for his enemies. The third is planting. The conspirators want to destroy 'the tree with its fruit,' 11:19, an echo of the olive tree of 11:16-17, while the wicked are said to have been planted and taken root, 12:2. The fourth is betrayal. The wicked of 12:1 are called faithless, and in 12:6 the prophet's brothers 'have betrayed' him, and the Hebrew uses one root for both.

The reply in 12:5 is deliberately severe. It is two questions about running, and neither one answers the question Jeremiah asked. The poem that follows then reveals that God is also a wounded party, with 'My house,' 'My inheritance,' 'My vineyard,' 'My plot of ground' and 'My pleasant field' all in a few verses. The chapter closes with an unexpected turn to hope, in which the language of uprooting and planting from Jeremiah's call, 1:10, returns for the nations.
context.historical:
Anathoth lay a few miles northeast of Jerusalem in the land of Benjamin, and it had been a priestly town since Joshua's day, Joshua 21:18. Jeremiah begins his book by naming himself 'one of the priests in Anathoth,' Jeremiah 1:1. Its priestly families may have descended from Abiathar, whom Solomon sent away to his fields in Anathoth when he removed him from the priesthood, 1 Kings 2:26-27. If so, Jeremiah's neighbours belonged to a line that had lost its place at the centre of worship, and to a family with long memories. Josiah's reform had also moved worship away from local sanctuaries, 2 Kings 23:8-9, and it is possible that country priests resented the prophet who spoke in the name of the covenant that had cost them standing. The text itself does not say, so the motive is an inference. What it does say is that the threat was 'You must not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand,' 11:21.

Jeremiah never forgot the town. Years later, with Babylon at the gate, he bought a field in Anathoth from his cousin Hanamel as a sign that Judah would one day be restored, Jeremiah 32:6-9. And when the exiles came home, 128 men of Anathoth were among them, Ezra 2:23. God's verdict that there would be 'no remnant,' 11:23, applies to the men who conspired, in the year of their punishment, and the town itself is not wiped from history.

The 'evil neighbours' of 12:14 and the 'beasts of the field' of 12:9 fit the years when raiders descended on Judah. Under Jehoiakim the LORD sent Chaldean, Aramean, Moabite and Ammonite bands against the kingdom, 2 Kings 24:2. The 'shepherds' of 12:10 might be foreign commanders, who are pictured as shepherds with their flocks in Jeremiah 6:3, or Judah's own rulers, whom Jeremiah blames elsewhere, Jeremiah 10:21 and 23:1.

The complaint about the prosperity of the wicked was an old one in Israel. Job asks why the wicked grow old and increase in power, Job 21:7, the psalmist envied them until he went into the sanctuary, Psalm 73:3 and 73:16-17, and Malachi records the people saying that evildoers prosper, Malachi 3:15. Jeremiah brings the argument into the courtroom.
context.canonical:
Jeremiah's confessions stand with the laments of the Psalms and the questions of Job and Habakkuk as scripture's way of showing that honest protest is a form of faith. The complaint in 12:1 is the question of Psalm 73:3, Job 21:7 and Habakkuk 1:13, but Jeremiah addresses it to the very One who has called him. The answer in 12:5 has its nearest parallel in Job 38 to 41, where God replies to a questioner with questions about creation, and in Jeremiah 15:19-21, where God tells the prophet that if he returns he will stand in God's presence and that He will make him a wall of bronze.

The image of the lamb joins Jeremiah to the servant of Isaiah 53. The conspirators' wish to 'cut him off from the land of the living,' 11:19, uses the same phrase as Isaiah 53:8, 'He was cut off from the land of the living,' and in 53:7 the servant is 'led like a lamb to the slaughter.' Isaiah's picture of the servant who bears the sin of others finds an early shadow in a prophet who suffers for the words he carries.

Hosea 9:15 speaks of hating and no longer loving a rebellious people, and Jeremiah 12:8 uses the same language of 'hate' for a beloved that has turned on her Lord. The theme of uprooting and replanting is the thread of Jeremiah's call, 1:10, 18:7-10 and 45:4. The oracles against the nations later include restoration for Moab and Ammon, 48:47 and 49:6, fulfilling the pattern of 12:15.

The New Testament takes up all of this. Jesus is rejected in His hometown, and He says that a prophet is without honour among his relatives and in his own household, Mark 6:4 and Luke 4:24-29, while John notes that even His own brothers did not believe in Him, John 7:5. Peter says He entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath, Romans 12:19, and Revelation puts Jeremiah's 'how long' on the lips of the martyrs, Revelation 6:10. Ephesians 2:12-19 shows the nations brought near, which is 12:15-16 in its fullest form.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The editors who placed this confession at the head of Jeremiah's private prayers wanted readers to see the man behind the oracles. For many chapters he has been the voice of judgment. Here he is a person who has just found out that his neighbours want him dead and who does what believers are meant to do with such news: he takes it to God. By recording his complaint, and God's sharp reply, the book teaches that the prophet is not an unfeeling mouthpiece. He pays for the message.

The passage also means to answer the problem of the wicked who prosper, but only partly. God does not give a philosophical solution. He tells Jeremiah that the hard road lies ahead, 12:5, and that the family betrayal he has just discovered is only the start, 12:6. This is not unkindness. It prepares him for what he will face, and it teaches him that faith has to be strong enough for horses and not only for foot races.

And it means to correct a narrow view of the suffering. Jeremiah thought of the injustice as his. God replies by showing that the injustice is also His: His house abandoned, His vineyard trampled, His beloved roaring against Him. The reader is invited to see sin as grief to God before it is trouble to us. The ending then widens the frame to the nations, so that hearers who thought God's concern ended at Judah's borders learn that its compassion does not.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a particular plot, a particular man's complaint, and a particular answer. It does not promise that those who oppose faithful servants will be struck down exactly as Jeremiah asks, and it does not make the request 'let me see Your vengeance' a pattern for believers to repeat about their enemies. The New Testament teaches the opposite emphasis: 'Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath,' Romans 12:19, and 'love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,' Matthew 5:44.

What carries forward is the permission to bring raw questions to God, with the assumption that He is righteous, 12:1. The shape of the prayer, 'Righteous are You ... yet I wish to contend,' is a model of how to complain without contempt. The reply is also instructive. God does not dispute Jeremiah's observation, since the wicked do prosper. He redirects him to the call, with its cost, and to the fact that God shares his grief. Believers who wrestle with injustice are meant to hold on in the same way, not abandoning the question but placing it where God will answer it, which Psalm 73:17 shows is in His presence.

debates.question: Is Jeremiah's request for vengeance in 11:20 and 12:3 a prayer to imitate?

views.label: A righteous appeal for justice
views.case: Jeremiah says he has committed his cause to God and does not take revenge himself. Similar cries appear in Psalm 109, in Revelation 6:10, and even in Paul's remark about Alexander in 2 Timothy 4:14. On this view the prayer is the voice of the righteous asking the Judge of all the earth to act.

views.label: An incomplete prayer that Christ corrects
views.case: Jesus teaches love for enemies, Matthew 5:44, and prays for His executioners, Luke 23:34, as Stephen does for his, Acts 7:60. On this view Jeremiah's cry belongs to an earlier stage of revelation and is gently reshaped. The book itself, in 15:19, tells Jeremiah that he must return from words like these if he is to be God's spokesman.

views.label: An honest confession that God answers by correction
views.case: Because it is a confession, the prayer shows what is in Jeremiah's heart, not what he ought to feel. God neither rebukes nor grants the request. He simply sets before Jeremiah a harder road, which suggests that honesty is welcome even where the content is not perfect.

debates.bearing: Taken together, the views agree that vengeance is God's, and that bringing even an imperfect prayer to Him is better than nursing it alone. The cross shows how God Himself deals with enemies, by bearing judgment before He gives mercy.

debates.question: What is God's answer in 12:5-6: rebuke, promotion, or comfort?

views.label: A rebuke
views.case: God does not answer the question and instead implies that Jeremiah's complaint is a failure of stamina. The one who has stumbled in a 'peaceful land' will not manage in the thickets of the Jordan, where lions live, as Jeremiah 49:19 suggests. The reply puts him in his place.

views.label: A summons to a larger calling
views.case: The questions treat Jeremiah as a runner who is being called to race horses. The point is not that he has failed but that God is about to ask more of him, and 15:19-21 later makes the same promise that God will make him a wall of bronze. The reply is a kind of promotion.

views.label: A comfort in disguise
views.case: By telling Jeremiah that his brothers have betrayed him, God shows that He already knows what Jeremiah knows, and He warns him not to trust the family's flattery. To be told the truth is itself a mercy.

debates.bearing: The reply refuses to treat the problem as merely theoretical. God draws Jeremiah deeper into the cost of faithfulness, and that is how He answers Habakkuk and Job as well.

debates.question: Do 12:14-17 promise salvation for the nations or only a return from exile?

views.label: The return of exiles alone
views.case: The 'evil neighbours' are uprooted from their land and God promises to bring 'each one to his inheritance,' 12:15. The text is about the nations being allowed to go home. 'Established among My people' means living alongside Israel on their own terms.

views.label: A conditional invitation to true belonging
views.case: The nations are to 'diligently learn the ways of My people and swear by My name,' 12:16, which is the vocabulary of conversion. Isaiah 19:24-25 goes further and calls Egypt 'My people' and Assyria 'My handiwork.' Verse 17 states the alternative: if they refuse, they are destroyed. Jeremiah 18:7-10 supplies the principle that God's announcements depend on repentance.

views.label: Both, with the second fulfilled in Christ
views.case: The nations' return to their land is the near horizon and their inclusion among God's people is the far one, as Ephesians 2:12-19 explains when it says that those once far off are now 'fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household.'

debates.bearing: The passage is clearly an offer. God declares that even those who have raided His inheritance may be rebuilt among His people if they turn and swear by His name, and the New Testament shows how wide that door finally opened.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb 'know' in 11:18 and 12:3 is yada, and it frames the prayer. 'The LORD informed me, so I knew' is literally 'made me know,' and 'You know me' answers it. The prophet is a man who knows because he has been told, and he asks God to examine what He knows. In 11:20 God 'examines the heart and mind,' and the footnote says the Hebrew is literally 'the kidneys.' The kidneys were the seat of deep feeling and conscience, and the line in 12:2 is correspondingly sharper: 'You are ever on their lips, but far from their hearts,' where the footnote again reads 'their kidneys.' The wicked say the right words, and nothing inside them is near God.

In 11:19 the plotters say, 'Let us destroy the tree with its fruit.' The Hebrew word behind 'fruit' is literally 'its bread' or 'its food,' and the ancient Greek translators rendered the phrase as 'let us put wood into his bread.' Early Christian writers heard that as a foreshadowing of the cross. The Hebrew does not say that, but the phrase 'cut him off from the land of the living' is the same one used of the servant in Isaiah 53:8.

The verb of 12:1, 'contend,' is rib, the word of a legal dispute, and the verse sets it beside 'righteous,' so the tone is that of a plaintiff who begins by granting the judge's justice. The word 'faithless' in 12:1 and the word 'betrayed' in 12:6 are forms of the same root, bagad. The people who live at ease are not strangers; they are the family. In 12:3 the request to 'set them apart' uses the verb of consecration, qadash, usually said of what is set apart for God. Jeremiah asks that the wicked be consecrated for slaughter, as a sacrificial animal is. It turns the language of worship into the language of judgment.

In 12:5 the 'thickets of the Jordan' are the dense growth along the river where lions lurked, as the phrase is used in Jeremiah 49:19. The reply that follows in 12:8 has the inheritance behaving like a lion, 'she has roared against Me,' and the text literally says she has 'given her voice' against God, with the same verb of giving. And the 'hate' of 12:8 is the language of covenant rejection, not hatred in the modern sense. Genesis 29:31 uses the same idea when it says Leah was 'unloved.' God is withdrawing love from a people that is behaving like an enemy, as Hosea 9:15 shows.

The family of verbs in 12:7 and 12:14 deserves a word. God says 'I have forsaken My house' and 'abandoned My inheritance' in 12:7, and the word for 'abandoned' is a different root from the word for 'uproot' in 12:14, but the two sound close and are set not far apart. What has been abandoned will be uprooted, and what is uprooted will be pitied: the sequence is spelled out in 12:15, 'I will once again have compassion on them,' and the word for compassion is related to the word for a mother's womb.

In 12:16 the nations will be 'established' among God's people. The word is literally 'built,' the second half of the pair of verbs in Jeremiah's call, 'to build and plant,' 1:10. The same verbs of uprooting and building that opened the book are used for the nations here.

typology.type: The lamb led to slaughter, cut off from the land of the living, Jeremiah 11:19
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah's own words, 'cut him off from the land of the living,' are the words used of the servant in Isaiah 53:8, and 'like a lamb led to slaughter' is Isaiah 53:7. John the Baptist says of Jesus, 'Look, the Lamb of God,' John 1:29. The correspondence is real but the contrast is sharp. Jeremiah did not know the plot, whereas Jesus, 'knowing all that was coming upon Him,' went out to meet His captors, John 18:4. Jeremiah's suffering was for his message, and Christ's was for the sins of others, which is why the type falls short.

typology.type: The prophet rejected by his own town and family, Jeremiah 11:21 and 12:6
typology.fulfillment: The men of Anathoth threaten the prophet, and his own father's household betrays him. Jesus' townspeople at Nazareth drive Him out and try to throw Him from a cliff, Luke 4:28-29. He says a prophet is without honour in his own household, Mark 6:4, and His brothers did not believe in Him, John 7:5. The pattern is that the messenger of God meets rejection from those closest to him. The type falls short because Jeremiah is rejected for being a prophet, while Jesus is rejected as the one to whom prophets pointed.

typology.type: God's grief over His house and vineyard, Jeremiah 12:7-10
typology.fulfillment: God's anguished 'My house, My vineyard, My beloved' finds an echo in Jesus weeping over Jerusalem, 'how often I have longed to gather your children together,' Luke 13:34, and in Luke 19:41. Isaiah 5:1-7 uses the same vineyard picture, and Jesus applies it in the parable of the tenants who kill the owner's son, Matthew 21:33-39. The escalation is that the Owner does not only lament His vineyard. He sends His own Son into it. The pattern is not a prediction, but the New Testament uses the same images.

typology.type: Uprooted nations rebuilt among God's people, Jeremiah 12:14-16
typology.fulfillment: The nations that attacked Israel are offered a place among God's people if they will learn God's ways and swear by His name. Ephesians 2:12-19 says Gentiles who were 'strangers to the covenants of the promise' have been brought near through the blood of Christ and are now 'fellow citizens with the saints.' Swearing by the LORD becomes confessing that 'Jesus is Lord,' Romans 10:9. The correspondence is that enemies become family. The type is only partial: Jeremiah's offer is conditional on learning Israel's ways, while Christ makes one new people from both.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ most plainly by the suffering of the one who speaks. Jeremiah is a prophet whose people plot to 'cut him off from the land of the living,' 11:19, and the phrase is the very one Isaiah uses of the Suffering Servant, 'He was cut off from the land of the living; He was stricken for the transgression of My people,' Isaiah 53:8. Jeremiah's suffering is not substitutionary, but the Bible's careful readers have heard in his experience the shape of what happens to God's messenger when he speaks truth to those who prefer comfort. The Gospels record the same conspiracy against Jesus, who was not betrayed by strangers but by a circle of leaders: 'the chief priests and elders ... conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him,' Matthew 26:3-4.

The difference is as important as the likeness. Jeremiah 'did not know' the plot, until the LORD informed him. Jesus, 'knowing all that was coming upon Him,' stepped forward to meet it, John 18:4. Jeremiah asks to see God's vengeance, while Jesus prays, 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34, and 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23, the same entrusting that Jeremiah does at the end of 11:20 when he says he has committed his cause to God. Peter's language shows how the apostles read the prophet: Jeremiah's posture of committing his case to God finds its fullest expression in the Son.

It leads to Christ by the divine title in 11:20. The LORD is the God who 'examines the heart and mind.' In Revelation 2:23 the risen Jesus says, 'I am the One who searches minds and hearts,' using the very words Jeremiah applied to God. The New Testament thus takes this attribute and puts it on the lips of Christ without argument. Likewise John says that Jesus 'knew what was in a man,' John 2:24-25. The Judge to whom Jeremiah entrusts his cause is the Son.

It leads to Christ by the hometown betrayal. Jeremiah's own brothers and father's household turned against him, 12:6. Jesus' own townspeople tried to throw Him off a cliff, Luke 4:28-29, and 'even His own brothers did not believe in Him,' John 7:5. Mark says He was without honour among His relatives and in His own household, Mark 6:4. A messenger who is rejected by his own is a pattern the Gospels pick up for Jesus.

And it leads to Christ by the grief of God. In 12:7 God says He has 'given the love of My life into the hands of her enemies.' We cannot say that Jeremiah foresaw the cross here, but the New Testament uses the same language of giving up: God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32, and the Son of Man 'is betrayed into the hands of sinners,' Matthew 26:45. The beloved is given over to enemies in Jeremiah as the penalty for sin. In the gospel the Beloved is given over so that enemies can be made family, as 12:15 to 17 hints and Ephesians 2:13 declares.

A caution: Jeremiah is not a disguised Christ, and not every detail of his confession is typological. The links rest on the New Testament's own use of Isaiah 53, its use of Jeremiah's divine title, and its record of Jesus' rejection, and they should be held at that strength.
study.god:
The God of this passage is the one who tells His servant what is happening and then allows him to speak. 'The LORD informed me, so I knew' means that God does not leave His prophet in the dark about the dangers around him, and the whole conversation shows that He permits protest. Jeremiah begins by granting His righteousness, 12:1, and nothing in the reply tells him to stop asking. A faith that cannot question is not the faith of this book.

God is the examiner of hearts. The kidneys and the heart, which Hebrew thought of as the seat of feeling and will, are open to Him, 11:20 and 12:3. He is able to see that the people honour Him with their lips while their inner life is far away, 12:2, and to see that Jeremiah's own heart is turned toward Him. Hidden things are therefore neither safe for the wicked nor lost to the righteous. The people's claim that 'He cannot see what our end will be,' 12:4, is exactly wrong.

God is just and also the Lord of timing. He promises judgment on Anathoth, 11:22-23, and on the nations, 12:14, but He does not tell Jeremiah when the wicked will be dragged away, and He does not explain why they flourish in the meantime. Scripture elsewhere gives the reason in part: He is patient, Jeremiah 18:7-10 shows that His announcements respond to repentance, and the end of the matter is known to Him, Psalm 73:17. A God who runs justice on a schedule we cannot see is not therefore unjust.

He is also wounded. The most surprising part of the chapter is the poem in 12:7 to 13, where God speaks as one who has been betrayed. He calls Judah 'the love of My life,' and then says that she has roared against Him and that He hates her. The language of hate here is the language of a love that has been spurned and has withdrawn, as the 'unloved' Leah shows in Genesis 29:31. His anger comes from His love and does not replace it. God's judgment is described as something He does with pain, giving up what He loves.

He is sovereign over the nations without being indifferent to them. The raiders and 'shepherds' who ravage Judah are His instruments, 12:9 and 12:12, and yet they will be held to account for their cruelty, 12:14. At the end He offers them compassion, 12:15, and a place among His people, 12:16. The same God who uproots is the God who builds, and His purposes reach far beyond one nation.

For worship, this chapter teaches us to pray honestly and to expect an answer that is more demanding than the one we asked for. It invites us to trust that the God who knows our hearts also feels the injury of sin, and that He keeps open a way back for His enemies as well as His friends.

crossReferences.note: The servant is 'led like a lamb to the slaughter' and 'cut off from the land of the living.' Jeremiah 11:19 uses both pictures of himself, and the shared phrase 'the land of the living' shows a shared vocabulary for the righteous sufferer, which Christian readers have long seen reaching its fullest form in the Servant.

The call of Jeremiah gives him authority over nations 'to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant.' The oracle in 12:14-17 is that commission in action, with uprooting for the nations followed by compassion and building. It shows that the final word of Jeremiah's ministry is planting.

God answers Jeremiah's next complaint with a conditional call: if he returns, God will restore him and make him a wall of bronze against those who fight him. It shows how the reply in 12:5 develops, since the harder road is paired with a promise of deliverance.

The psalmist envied the arrogant until he went into God's sanctuary and discerned their end. This is the nearest Old Testament answer to Jeremiah 12:1. It adds that the problem of the prospering wicked is settled by seeing things from God's presence, and not by new information about the present.

Habakkuk asks how long he must cry for help and why God tolerates injustice. His complaint is close to Jeremiah's and receives a similar answer, that God is doing something larger than the prophet can see. Both books show faith expressed as protest.

God says that for the wickedness of their deeds He will drive them from His house and no longer love them. This is the same language of 'hate' and expulsion as in Jeremiah 12:7-8, and Hosea shows that such words describe a broken covenant relationship, a love spurned and withdrawn.

Jesus says no prophet is accepted in his hometown, and the people of Nazareth drive Him out and try to throw Him over the cliff. It is the Anathoth plot of Jeremiah 11:21 in the life of Christ, and it shows that rejection by one's own people belongs to the prophets' path.

The risen Christ says, 'I am the One who searches minds and hearts.' This applies to Jesus the language of Jeremiah 11:20 and 17:10, where it belongs to the LORD. The apostles identify the Judge Jeremiah called on with the Son.

When Jesus suffered, He did not retaliate but entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly. This is the New Testament's picture of what Jeremiah does in 11:20 when he commits his cause to God, but carried through to the end without a request for vengeance.

Believers are told not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath, citing 'Vengeance is Mine.' The principle clarifies Jeremiah's prayer: he does not strike his enemies but hands them to God, which is the posture Paul commends.

Gentiles once without hope and without God are brought near through the blood of Christ and become fellow citizens with the saints. This is the New Testament fulfillment of Jeremiah 12:15-16, where uprooted nations are rebuilt among God's people.

Israel joins Egypt and Assyria as a blessing in the earth, and God calls them 'My people,' 'My handiwork,' and 'My inheritance.' It parallels Jeremiah 12:14-16 by using the word inheritance for nations that were once enemies and shows that Jeremiah's promise has Old Testament company.

Joseph's brothers saw him from afar and plotted to kill him. The betrayal of Jeremiah 12:6 by his own father's household follows the older pattern of the righteous one rejected by his family, which also runs on through the Psalms to Christ.

study.oneStory:
The details of this passage already belong to the first chapters of the Bible. When God says that Judah has 'sown wheat but harvested thorns,' 12:13, He is describing the curse of Genesis 3:18, thorns and thistles in the ground. The land that 'mourns,' 12:4, is the earth groaning under the sentence on human sin. Jeremiah's neighbours also play a very old role: the brothers who hate and plot, like Cain with Abel, Genesis 4:8, and Joseph's brothers in Genesis 37:18. The righteous sufferer who is betrayed by his own is one of the oldest figures in the story.

The story goes on to ask what God will do about it. His answer, as this chapter hints, is to take the suffering into Himself. The poem of 12:7 to 13 shows God not as a distant magistrate but as a wounded owner who has given up the love of His life. That is the same God who, in Genesis 3, comes looking for the guilty and clothes them. The one who uproots also keeps compassion in reserve, and at the end of the chapter He announces that He will return each exile to his inheritance and rebuild even the nations.

In the middle of the Bible, the figure of the faithful sufferer grows. Jeremiah is rejected by his hometown, Isaiah's servant is led like a lamb to the slaughter, the psalmists cry for rescue from enemies who were once friends, and then Jesus comes to a town where He is rejected and to a Jerusalem where He is killed. In Him the lamb is more than a picture: He is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, John 1:29. The wound that Jeremiah describes, a prophet cut off from the land of the living, becomes the wound that heals, since Christ was 'cut off from the land of the living' for the transgression of His people, Isaiah 53:8. He is raised, and the cut-off tree begins to grow again.

The promise to the nations is also part of the main line. God's blessing to Abraham was that all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3. Jeremiah's offer in 12:15 to 16 to build the nations among God's people looks ahead to that, and the apostles declare that Gentiles are now fellow citizens with the saints, Ephesians 2:19. The story ends with 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4, with the nations walking by the light of the city, Revelation 21:24, and with the tree of life whose leaves are for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2. The land that mourned, the wicked who prospered, the lamb who was slaughtered, and the vineyard once trampled are all answered at last.

sermon.title: Christmas at the Castle, Part 3
sermon.why: Carson works through Jeremiah 11:18 to 12:17 in detail, reading Jeremiah's complaint about the prosperity of the wicked and God's response, exactly the confession and answer this study examines.

quiz.q: What does Jeremiah compare himself to in 11:19, describing his ignorance of the plot against him?

options.text: A gentle lamb led to slaughter, not knowing they had plotted against him.
options.note: Verse 19 states this image directly.

options.text: A lion protecting its territory from attackers.
options.note: This is the opposite image; Jeremiah pictures himself as vulnerable and unsuspecting, not fierce.

options.text: A soldier armed and ready for battle.
options.note: This contradicts the picture of unsuspecting vulnerability the text actually describes.

options.text: A shepherd searching for a lost sheep.
options.note: Not the image used; Jeremiah is the vulnerable one being led away, not the one searching.

quiz.q: What specific complaint does Jeremiah bring to God in 12:1?

options.text: Why does the way of the wicked prosper, and why do all the faithless live at ease?
options.note: Verse 1 states this complaint directly.

options.text: Why did God allow the temple to be built in the first place?
options.note: Not the complaint raised in this verse; the temple is not the subject here.

options.text: Why did God choose him rather than someone else as prophet?
options.note: Jeremiah questions his call elsewhere, but that is not this specific complaint.

options.text: Why does the land continue to suffer drought?
options.note: Drought becomes the subject later in chapters 14-15, not the complaint raised here.

quiz.q: What does God call Judah in 12:7, expressing His own grief?

options.text: My house, My inheritance, the love of My life given into her enemies' hands.
options.note: Verse 7 uses exactly this intimate, grieving language.

options.text: An enemy He had always opposed from the beginning.
options.note: The text expresses grief over betrayed love, not original enmity.

options.text: A distant nation with no prior covenant relationship.
options.note: This contradicts the entire premise of covenant intimacy running through this passage.

options.text: A stranger who had never truly belonged to Him.
options.note: This contradicts the possessive, intimate language of verse 7, My house, My inheritance.

quiz.q: Who does God say has betrayed Jeremiah, even close to home, according to 12:6?

options.text: Even his own brothers and his father's household have betrayed him and cried aloud against him.
options.note: Verse 6 states this plainly.

options.text: No one at all; Jeremiah faced no betrayal from anyone.
options.note: This directly contradicts the passage's account of betrayal.

options.text: Foreign kings who sought to conquer Judah.
options.note: The betrayal described in this verse comes from close family, not foreign powers.

options.text: Only distant strangers from neighboring towns.
options.note: The text specifically names Jeremiah's own brothers and household, not distant strangers.

quiz.q: What hope does God hold out even for the wicked neighboring nations in 12:14-17?

options.text: If they diligently learn the ways of His people and swear by His name, they will be established among His people.
options.note: Verse 16 states this conditional hope plainly.

options.text: That God has no further dealings with any nation beyond Israel.
options.note: This contradicts the passage, which explicitly addresses these surrounding nations directly.

options.text: That they will be destroyed with no possibility of restoration whatsoever.
options.note: This contradicts verses 15 to 16, which hold out compassion and possible restoration.

options.text: That they will permanently inherit the land of Judah.
options.note: The passage describes uprooting and possible restoration to their own land, not permanent inheritance of Judah's territory.

questions: Jeremiah did not even suspect that his own townspeople were plotting against him. Has faithfulness to God ever cost you a relationship you did not expect to lose?

Jeremiah brought his honest complaint, why do the wicked prosper, directly to God rather than suppressing it. Where do you need to bring an honest complaint to God instead of masking it with false peace?
God says His own heart grieves over Judah, His beloved inheritance turned against Him. How does knowing God feels real grief over sin change the way you picture Him this week?

God's answer to Jeremiah's complaint was, in effect, you have not seen anything yet, calling him to deeper endurance rather than an easy explanation. How do you tend to respond when God's answer to your prayers is not the explanation you wanted?
Even here, God promises compassion and restoration to nations who turn to Him. Where do you need to trust that God's compassion can reach further than you currently believe?

translationNotes.note: The gentle lamb image directly anticipates Isaiah 53:7's servant song, later applied explicitly to Christ in Acts 8:32 and John 1:29.
The verb rendered contend is the same legal term used for covenant lawsuits elsewhere in the prophets, framing Jeremiah's complaint as a formal appeal to God's own justice.
The Hebrew behind speckled bird of prey is genuinely obscure and variously rendered across translations, but every reading pictures Judah as marked out for attack by surrounding predators.
